planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average garden soil in partial to full shade; Royalty spreads by surface stolons and fills in within a season or two once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in partial to full shade, where Royalty forms a low, dense mat of deeply crinkled, heavily textured foliage in a rich mahogany-red that holds its color well through the growing season. In May and June, upright spikes of vivid blue flowers rise several inches above the crinkled leaves, giving a strong color contrast that makes this cultivar stand out among other dark-leaved ajugas. Its compact stature and modest spread make it a good choice for edging paths, tucking between stepping stones, or filling small shaded pockets where a larger-spreading ajuga would quickly overrun its neighbors. Divide congested patches in spring or fall every few years to maintain vigor and to generate new starts for other shaded areas.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Arctic Fox Ajuga (White-Margined Grey-Green Variegated Bugleweed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Arctic Fox arose as a sport of 'Silver Queen' and carries the same tendency to produce occasional plain-green reversion shoots that should be removed to keep the variegation strong.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where Arctic Fox's spoon-shaped leaves display irregular white-to-cream margins over a grey-green and dark green center, giving the groundcover a frosted, variegated look that brightens dim corners. Whorls of small, dark bluish-purple flowers appear on short spikes in May and June, adding a brief seasonal accent to the foliage display. Because it originated as a mutation on 'Silver Queen', occasional stems can revert to solid green; cut these out as soon as they appear so they do not outcompete the variegated growth. Light afternoon shade helps keep the pale leaf margins from scorching in hot climates, while a bit more sun in cooler regions can deepen the purple flower color.
sources: U.S. Plant Patent PP8,395 (Ajuga reptans 'Arctic Fox', H. A. Ross)

common_name: Purple Chablis Lamium (Silver-and-Green Lavender-Purple Dead Nettle)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; Purple Chablis is self-cleaning and needs no deadheading to keep flowering through the season.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where Purple Chablis forms a low, spreading mat of silver-and-green marbled foliage topped through spring and summer with soft lavender-purple flowers. Compared to older lamium selections it tolerates more heat without the foliage burning or thinning out in a Southern summer, and it keeps flowering without deadheading. Use it as a trailing groundcover under shrubs and shaded perennials, as an edging plant along a shaded path, or as a spiller in mixed shade containers where its variegated foliage can cascade over the rim. Give it consistent moisture during the first season to establish a full root system, after which established plantings tolerate brief dry spells better than many other dead nettle cultivars.
